steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Unemployment will soon decrease.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
If total govt spending significantly goes up, unemployment will decrease.

If total govt spending significantly decreases, unemployment will decrease.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
We know the first claim is the conclusion because the other two claims are clearly built to work together. Connectors like and, but, and on the other hand show two claims interacting to move the argument forward.

Each conditional premise has TWO outcomes, and one of them is decreasing unemployment. I didn't bother writing out the other half of each outcome, because all we care about is proving that unemployment will decrease.

At first, this argument seems pretty reasonable. It looks like an *Either Way You Slice It* argument: whether spending increases significantly or decreases significantly, we end up with lower unemployment, so either way unemployment goes down.

But an argument on Sufficient Assumption can't *already* be airtight. There has to be a gap, so that the correct answer can close it.

So let's argue with the economist. How could unemployment *fail to decrease*?

Spending doesn't have to go significantly up or significantly down. It could stay about the same. Then neither rule is triggered, and the premises tell us nothing about unemployment.

The economist is presenting a *False Choice* (a false dichotomy), treating a big increase and a big decrease as the only two options while ignoring the middle ground where spending barely moves.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
We need to rule out the middle ground. Predict an answer saying that next year government spending will either significantly increase or significantly decrease.

With that fact in hand, one of the two rules has to fire, and both rules end at lower unemployment. Whenever an argument covers two cases that lead to the same result, the sufficient assumption is often the one that guarantees one of those cases actually happens.

notes.body:
The economist covers two cases: spending goes up significantly, or spending goes down significantly. Both lead to lower unemployment. But nothing says one of those two things will happen. Spending could stay about the same, and then neither rule applies.

This answer closes that gap. If spending will either rise or fall significantly, one of the two cases must happen, and either way unemployment decreases. The conclusion follows. On the next either-way argument, check whether the cases listed are really the only options, and look for the answer that makes them the only options.

B tells us officials intend to reduce unemployment, but intentions don't guarantee results. B says nothing about whether spending will significantly rise or fall, so the middle case, where spending stays about the same, is still open.

C links demand for workers to lower unemployment, but the premises already get us to lower unemployment in both spending cases. The gap is whether one of those cases happens at all. Since C doesn't tell us whether spending will go up or down, it doesn't do the job we need it to do.

D talks about the long run, while the conclusion is that unemployment will soon decrease. Even if the economy slows years from now, that tells us nothing about next year. And D still doesn't say whether spending will significantly go up or down, so the middle case stays open.

E sounds connected because it uses both mechanisms from the premises. But diagram it: unemployment decreases → economy stimulated or businesses retain earnings. That tells us what is required for unemployment to fall, not that either requirement will be met. A rule that can only lead to "will not decrease" can never prove that unemployment will decrease.

why: Breakdown and A to C notes were sound, but the Evaluate step used a gendered pronoun for the economist, the Goal named only the task, and the D and E notes were verdict-thin (E never diagrammed the rule).

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Most children under six are egocentric and selfish in their attitudes toward animals.

Ordinarily, children only begin to understand that animals are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs somewhere between the ages of six and nine. So most children under six do not yet understand this.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Most children should not have pets until they are at least six years old.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Look at the conclusion's key word: "should." The evidence only describes what young children are like. The conclusion tells us what ought to happen. That "should not have pets" idea is a new concept in the conclusion, and on Sufficient Assumption the correct answer almost always has to supply it.

Let's argue with the psychologist. Given that most children under six don't yet understand that animals have their own feelings and needs, how could we argue that they should still have pets? Easy: maybe a child doesn't need to understand that to have a pet. A parent could do the caring, and the child could learn along the way. The argument never rules that out.

We can sketch it with arrows, as long as we remember the premise says "Ordinarily," so it is a "most" claim, not an "all" claim:

under 6 → not understand (most of them)
not understand → should not have pet (missing)

If every child who doesn't understand should not have a pet, then the "most" in the premise carries straight through: most children under six should not have pets.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
We're looking for a rule that says children who don't understand that animals are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs should not have pets:

not understand → should not have pet

The contrapositive is just as good: should have pet → understand. Expect it to be worded with "only," since "only" marks the right side of the arrow. A rule linking "egocentric and selfish" to "should not have pets" would also work, because that premise is about the same group of children.

notes.body: A is about who takes care of the pet, and it never says what any child should or should not have. A sufficient assumption has to deliver the conclusion's new idea, "should not have pets." Combine A with the premises and you still can't say a word about what children should do.

Diagram it: understand → should be allowed to have pets. Our under-sixes mostly don't understand, so B's trigger never fires for them. B is the reversal of the rule we need (should have pets → understand). Knowing that children who understand may have pets says nothing about whether children who don't understand may have them too.

C says what is the case: most egocentric and selfish children "do not have pets." The conclusion is about what should be the case. A fact about who currently owns pets can't prove that anyone ought not to own one. No "should" goes in, so no "should" comes out.

D is tempting because it sounds like the premises, but that is the problem: it repeats the evidence (egocentric, doesn't understand) and adds nothing about what children should do. Stacking more evidence of the same kind never closes a gap to a "should" conclusion. Ask of every answer here: does it contain "should not have pets" or its contrapositive?

"The only children who should have pets are those who understand that their pets are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs." A sentence of the form The only X are Y means X → Y, so: should have pet → understand. Contrapositive: not understand → should not have pet.

Now chain it with the evidence. Most children under six → not understand → should not have pet. So most children under six should not have pets, which is the conclusion.

The move to repeat: find the new concept in the conclusion ("should not have pets"), then look for the rule that puts it on the right side of an arrow whose left side is something the evidence gives you.

why: PT157 explicit-Standard register: Evaluate restated the argument without objecting to it, the Evidence step dropped the egocentric premise, and the notes were padded, with an em dash in C and a muddled 'illegal negation' label on B.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
In an experiment with 200 randomly selected people, the half who were allowed to gesture spoke more quickly and repeated themselves less than the half who were not.

So gesturing went along with quicker speech and less repetition.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body:
Gesturing helps speakers quickly find the phrases they want.

Notice the new idea here: finding phrases. The experiment measured speed and repetition. Nobody measured how quickly anyone found a phrase.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Let's argue with the author. Given that the gesturers spoke faster and repeated themselves less, how could gesturing still not help them find phrases?

Maybe gesturing just speeds people up. Waving your hands could make you more animated without making the right words come any faster. Or maybe gesturers repeated themselves less because a gesture did some of the describing for them, so they didn't need to say it twice. Either way, the speech changed for a reason that has nothing to do with phrase-finding.

The author is assuming that quicker, less repetitive speech is a sign of finding phrases faster. On Sufficient Assumption, we don't need to argue about whether that is true. We just need the rule that makes it true:

gesturing → quicker speech, less repetition (evidence)
quicker speech, less repetition → helps find phrases (missing)

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for a rule whose trigger matches what the experiment showed about gesturing (it goes with quicker speech and less repetition) and whose outcome is the conclusion's new idea (helps speakers quickly find the phrases they want).

Expect a reversal trap: a rule that runs from helping find phrases to quicker speech. That direction starts from the thing we are trying to prove, so it can't prove it.

notes.body: Diagram A: speaking quickly with little repetition → gesturing. That connects speech and gesturing again, which the evidence already did, just in the other direction. It never mentions finding phrases, and a sufficient assumption has to bring the conclusion's new idea in. With A added, we still can't conclude anything about phrases.

B is about how the cartoons were chosen. At most, that makes the experiment look fairer. But a fairer experiment still only measured speed and repetition. B says nothing about finding phrases, so it can't make the conclusion follow.

C is the bridge we predicted. Its trigger, "Any form of behavior correlated with quicker speech and less repetition in speech," is exactly what the experiment showed about gesturing. Its outcome, helping speakers "find the phrases they want quickly," is exactly the conclusion.

Chain it: gesturing → correlated with quicker speech and less repetition → helps find phrases. Done.

Notice how low C sets the bar. It only asks for a correlation, which is all the experiment delivered. When the evidence is a study and the conclusion names something the study never measured, the sufficient assumption is usually a rule that turns what was measured into what was concluded.

D is the trap. Diagram it: helps find phrases → speak more quickly and repeat less. We need the opposite direction: quicker speech and less repetition → helps find phrases.

Here's why the direction matters. D tells us that anything that helps you find phrases will speed you up. It does not tell us that anything that speeds you up is helping you find phrases. Gesturing could speed people up for some other reason, like the animation idea in the Evaluate step, and D would still be true. D starts from the thing we are trying to prove, so it can never prove it.

E says that within the gesturing group, the fastest, least repetitive speakers gestured the most. That makes the link between gesturing and fluent speech more convincing. But it is still only about speed and repetition. Making the evidence stronger doesn't close the gap to finding phrases; on Sufficient Assumption, only a rule that reaches the conclusion's idea can do that.

why: No Evaluate step, a Goal that predicted an 'or' rule framed as speaking quickly helping find phrases, a junk-filled Conclusion step, and padded PT157 notes with em dashes.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Because television is in nearly every home, few children today spend their free time reading stories.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Few children today will develop a lifelong interest in literature.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence is about reading stories now. The conclusion is about a lifelong interest in literature. Those are different ideas.

Let's argue with the author. Given that few children read stories in their free time today, how could plenty of them still end up with a lifelong interest in literature? Easy: they could discover it later, in a high school English class or as adults. Nothing in the argument says the only road to loving literature runs through childhood story time.

To shut that down, we need reading stories to be required for a lifelong interest:

~ spend free time reading → ~ lifelong interest in lit

Why does that prove "few"? If interest requires reading, then everyone who develops the interest is inside the reading group. The reading group is small (few children), so the interested group can be no bigger. A rule in the other direction, reading → interest, would not cap the number at all.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
We'll keep our eyes open for the rule above or its contrapositive:

lifelong interest in lit → spend free time reading

Words like only or requires attached to reading stories are the giveaway. We can also eliminate any answer that doesn't include the idea of developing a lifelong interest in literature, because the answer has to bring that new idea in.

notes.body: "No children who spend their free time reading stories fail to develop a lifelong interest in literature." Cut the double negative: reads stories → lifelong interest. That makes reading enough for the interest, but we need it to be required. Test it: even if every child reader develops the interest, the many non-readers could develop it too, so the number is never capped at "few."

"Only those people who currently spend their free time reading stories will develop a lifelong interest in literature." "Only" marks the right side of the arrow: lifelong interest → currently reads stories. Contrapositive: doesn't read now → no lifelong interest.

Now the count works. Everyone who will develop the interest has to come from the reading group. Few children are in that group, so few children will develop the interest.

The move to repeat: to prove that few (or no) people will have X, make X require something few (or no) people have.

C diagrams as: no TV at home → reads stories. That's about reading and television only. It never mentions a lifelong interest in literature, so no combination of C and the evidence can reach the conclusion.

D is tempting because it finally mentions a lifelong interest in literature. But its trigger is watching "a great deal of television," and the evidence never says children do that. It says TV is everywhere and few children read. Without knowing most children are heavy watchers, D never fires, and it says nothing about children who don't read but don't watch much TV either.

E tells us that few child readers watch television. Like C, it stays inside reading and TV and never touches a lifelong interest in literature. An answer without the conclusion's new idea can't make the conclusion follow.

why: PT157 explicit-Standard register: Evaluate stated the missing rule without arguing against the author or explaining why the rule caps the count at 'few', and the notes were padded, repetitive and used em dashes.

steps.label: Conclusion (Thus)
steps.body: Most independent films do not have absolute integrity as works of art.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Indie filmmakers need to make profits, and this affects the artistic decisions made in creating most indie films.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Sufficient Assumption, once we've found the conclusion, we ask whether it contains a New Concept. If it does, the correct answer almost always brings that concept in.

This conclusion is trying to prove that most indie films "do not have absolute integrity." Did the filmmaker ever say what it takes to have absolute integrity, or what destroys it? No. So the correct answer must be a rule that lets us prove that a film does not have absolute integrity.

What do we know about most indie films? Their artistic decisions are affected by the need to make profits.

Let's argue with the filmmaker. Given that profit affects the artistic decisions behind most indie films, how could those films still have absolute integrity? Maybe a little profit pressure doesn't touch a film's integrity at all. The argument never says it does.

Notice the first sentence is just the view the filmmaker is pushing back on (people think indie films have more integrity because they are less conventional). It isn't support, so the answer doesn't need to deal with conventionality.

The "most" also carries through cleanly. If profit-affected decisions always mean no absolute integrity, then most indie films (the profit-affected ones) lack it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: A classic missing link correct answer would say that if the artistic decisions made in creating a film are affected by the need to make profits, then the film doesn't have absolute integrity as a work of art. They might surprise us with how the trigger is worded, but we're only interested in answers that provide a rule that puts not-absolute-integrity on the right side of the arrow, with profit-affected decisions on the left. Expect an illegal negation or a reversal of this rule as a trap. The correct answer might also come in contrapositive form: if a film does have absolute integrity, then its artistic decisions aren't affected by profit.

notes.body: Diagram A: decisions unaffected by profit → absolute integrity. That's the illegal negation of what we need (affected by profit → not absolute integrity). A only tells us about films free of profit pressure, and most indie films aren't, so A's trigger never fires for them. A is perfectly consistent with a profit-affected film having absolute integrity.

B is the rule we predicted. Its trigger, "If any of the artistic decisions made in creating something were affected by the need to make profits," matches the evidence about most indie films. Its outcome, "does not have absolute integrity as a work of art," is the conclusion.

Chain it: most indie films → profit-affected decisions → not absolute integrity. So most indie films lack absolute integrity.

Notice the word "any." It makes the trigger easy to hit: one profit-affected decision is enough. A sufficient assumption wants a trigger the evidence clearly satisfies and an outcome that is exactly the conclusion.

C compares individuals with groups "on average." The filmmaker never sorts filmmakers into individuals and groups, and a comparison of averages can't prove that any particular film lacks absolute integrity. C never connects profit to integrity, which is the gap.

D says unconventionality has "no bearing" on integrity. That undercuts the view in the first sentence, but knocking out one factor doesn't tell us what does destroy integrity. D gives us no rule that ends in "do not have absolute integrity," so the conclusion still doesn't follow.

E is the tempting one because it has the shape of a correct answer: "no integrity ... unless the artistic decisions made in creating it were unaffected." But read to the end: unaffected "by views about what is conventional," not by the need to make profits. The evidence says profit affected the decisions. It never says views about conventionality did. So E's trigger is never met, and it can't tell us anything about indie films. Always check that the trigger matches the evidence word for word in meaning.

why: PT158 explicit-Standard register with a fidelity error: the E note described E as being about profit when E is about views on what is conventional; notes were padded and used em dashes, and the Evaluate step claimed '99% of the time'.

steps.label: Conclusion (Thus)
steps.body: Wallakim Pond doesn't have a thriving population of turtles.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Thriving populations of turtles require conditions that are beneficial to turtles. Wallakim Pond has acidic water.

(Sosachi Pond's water is not acidic, but the conclusion is only about Wallakim, so Sosachi is just a contrast.)

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
We know Wallakim's water is acidic. We know that without beneficial conditions there's no thriving turtle population. But nothing connects acidity to beneficial conditions. For all the argument says, turtles might love acidic water.

So it looks like we just need to hear that acidic water is not a condition that is beneficial to turtles. If we don't hear that missing link intuitively, we can derive it by turning the Conclusion into an elongated logic path, checking which parts of that path the Evidence provides, and solving for the missing part as our Sufficient Assumption.
```
CONCLUSION
Wallakim -------------------------------> ~Thriving
Pond                                       Pop of T's
EVIDENCE
Wallakim --> acidic     Cond's --> ~Thriving
Pond         water      not ben    Pop of T's
MISSING LINK
acidic --> Cond's
water      not ben
```

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: We want an answer that conveys this rule: if there's acidic water, then the conditions are not beneficial to turtles. Its contrapositive works too: if conditions are beneficial, then the water is not acidic. Since only if introduces the right side of an arrow, the contrapositive version could easily show up as an only if statement about beneficial conditions. We'll also take any other answer that we could combine with our evidence to derive that Wallakim Pond doesn't have a thriving population of turtles.

notes.body: Diagram A: not acidic → beneficial. That's the illegal negation of the link we need (acidic → not beneficial). A tells us about ponds without acidic water, and Wallakim's water is acidic, so A's trigger never fires. A is perfectly consistent with acidic water also being beneficial to turtles.

Calling acidity the "most important factor" says acidity matters, but not which way. It never says acidic water is bad for turtles. Even if it were, other good conditions might still make Wallakim beneficial overall. We need a guarantee that acidic means not beneficial, and B doesn't give one.

C only ranks the two ponds. Wallakim's conditions could be less beneficial than Sosachi's and still be beneficial enough for turtles to thrive. A comparison can't tell us whether Wallakim clears the bar, and the conclusion is about Wallakim alone.

Diagram D: Wallakim not acidic → thriving. Its contrapositive is: not thriving → acidic. Neither version starts from "acidic," which is the fact we have. Test it: Wallakim could be thriving right now with acidic water, and it could also thrive if the acid were gone. D allows both, so it can't prove Wallakim isn't thriving.

"The conditions at a pond are beneficial to turtles only if the water in the pond is not acidic." The words only if introduce the right side: beneficial → not acidic. Contrapositive: acidic → not beneficial. That's our missing link.

Chain it with the evidence: Wallakim → acidic → not beneficial → not thriving. The conclusion follows.

The move to repeat: when the link you predicted doesn't appear in the choices, check for its contrapositive, and remember that "only if" points to the necessary side.

why: PT158 explicit-Standard register: notes were padded with em dashes, the A note garbled the illegal-negation explanation ('affirms the consequence'), and the D note never ran the logic on the fact we have.

steps.label: Conclusion (Thus)
steps.body:
Some government employees who work in the Hanson Building are computer programmers.
```
some HB are CP   or   HB <--s--> CP
```

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Most members of Bargaining Unit 17 (B17) are computer programmers.
```
most B17 are CP   or   B17 --m--> CP
```

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The blank comes right after "since," a support indicator, so whatever fills it is support for the conclusion announced by "Thus."

We need to prove that at least one government employee in the Hanson Building is a computer programmer. All we know is that most members of B17 are computer programmers. B17 is a unit of the government employees' union, so its members are government employees.

Let's argue with the author. Given that most B17 members are programmers, how could the Hanson Building have no programmers at all? Easy: none of those programmers work there. Nothing yet puts anyone from B17 in the building.

Computer programmers is the ingredient the premise and conclusion share, so the answer has to tie together the two dangling ingredients:

membership in Bargaining Unit 17
working in the Hanson Building

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Since we're trying to prove that some people in the Hanson Building are programmers, and we know that most people in B17 are programmers, we want an answer that puts B17 into the Hanson Building.

There's a precise version of this. When the premise is a "most" and the conclusion is a "some," think about the most + most inference:
```
Most A are B
+ Most A are C
=================
Some B are C
```
Why does it work? Picture B17 with 100 members. If at least 51 are programmers and at least 51 work in the Hanson Building, those two groups can't fit into 100 people without overlapping. At least 2 members have to be in both.

So we're predicting the other "most" about the same group:
```
Most B17 are programmers      prem
+ Most B17 are Hanson          answer
=================
Some Hanson are programmers    conc
```
Watch for a "most" that runs the wrong direction (most Hanson workers are B17). The two "most" statements have to be about the same group.

notes.body: A puts the non-programmer members of B17 in the Hanson Building, which is the wrong subgroup. Say B17 has 100 members: 70 programmers and 30 non-programmers. A puts about 20 of the 30 non-programmers in Hanson. All 70 programmers could still work elsewhere, so no programmer is guaranteed to be in the building.

The executive committee never appears in the argument, and nothing says its members are programmers. Test it: the committee could be made up entirely of B17's non-programmers. Then most of the committee works in Hanson and still no programmer does.

C is the tempting one because it links B17 and the Hanson Building, just in the wrong direction. C says "most of the government employees who work in the Hanson Building are members of Bargaining Unit Number 17." That is a "most" about Hanson workers, not about B17 members, so it doesn't pair with our premise.

Run numbers. B17 has 1,000 members: 700 programmers and 300 non-programmers. Hanson has 20 workers, and 15 of them are B17 non-programmers. Most Hanson workers are B17 members, and still no programmer works there. The two "most" statements must be about the same group to force an overlap.

D gives the second "most" about the same group. More than half of B17 are programmers (premise), and more than half of B17 work in the Hanson Building (D). Two groups that each take up more than half of B17 have to overlap, so at least one member is both a programmer and a Hanson worker. That person is a government employee who works in the Hanson Building and is a computer programmer, which is the conclusion.

The move to repeat: when a "most" premise has to produce a "some" conclusion, look for a second "most" about the same group.

E tells us most Hanson workers are government employees, but it never connects the building to B17 or to programmers. Government employees in Hanson could all be from other units with no programmers at all. With no tie to B17, there's no overlap to force.

why: PT158 explicit-Standard register with damage: the Goal carried a 'Supernerds' aside, an internal note line and a reference to an LSAT 'game', the evidence used unexplained shorthand, and the notes used em dashes and padding.

steps.label: Conclusion (we can thus conclude)
steps.body: Tea is no more popular now than it ever was.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The Survey Group, a neutral polling company, has tracked tea sales at numerous stores for the last 20 years and has found no change in the amount of tea sold.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
We're trying to argue that tea **is** more popular than before.
Barr will ask how there could be no change in the amount of tea sold at these numerous stores over the past 20 years. We could either make an excuse for that survey data (they measured the wrong thing, or the wrong places), or bring up other data that makes it sound like tea IS more popular.
Notice the jump: the evidence is about some stores; the conclusion is about tea's popularity in general. Whenever an argument rests on a survey, ask whether the sample represents the group in the conclusion.
Maybe the stores that are selling the most tea weren't even open 20 years ago, so they're not part of this comparison. Or maybe the surveyed stores are all in places where tea never caught on.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: We either want an answer that helps us argue that tea is more popular than before or an answer that makes an excuse for the author's evidence (i.e. if tea is more popular than before, then why is this survey showing no change in the amount of tea sold at these stores?)

notes.body: A survey the Association only plans to run next year gives us no data now. Announcing a survey isn't evidence of anything, and it doesn't touch the Survey Group's 20 years of flat sales. Even if the new survey comes out differently, A doesn't tell us that.

Being "generally receptive to the idea of trying new types of tea" is an attitude, not a purchase, and it isn't a change over time. The public could have been just as receptive 20 years ago. Barr's conclusion is about tea being more popular now than before, and B gives no before-and-after comparison.

C is trying to make us doubt the Survey Group. But why would consumer advocacy groups want tea sales to look flat? C gives no motive, and the stimulus calls the Survey Group neutral. Funding alone, with no reason to skew the data, doesn't weaken the survey.

This is the excuse for the survey data we predicted. If every surveyed store is "located in the same small region of the country," flat sales there tell us very little about the country as a whole. Tea could be booming everywhere else.

The move to repeat: when the evidence is a survey or a sample, weaken by showing the sample doesn't represent the group the conclusion is about.

E is the tempting one because an "expensive and efficient advertising campaign" sounds like it should boost popularity. But it tells us about effort, not results, and Barr's data says sales didn't move. If anything, E helps Barr: it explains the visibility the Association cited as paid advertising, so that visibility is weaker evidence that people actually like tea more.

why: Breakdown was sound (one em dash in Evidence), but all five choice notes were one-line verdicts with no test, and the popular advertising trap got no more attention than the others.
